sections.h: The book of Jonah in one page
sections.b: Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-hepher is named in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet who spoke for Jeroboam II. The book of Jonah tells a story about him: the LORD sends him to Nineveh, he runs to Tarshish, a storm and a lot expose him, a huge fish swallows him, he prays a psalm of thanks, and he finally goes to Nineveh. The city turns back, God changes his mind about the harm, and Jonah is angry. A plant, a worm and a wind lead to God's closing question (4:11). Jesus names "the sign of Jonah" (Matthew 12:38-41; Luke 11:29-32).

common: The book is a story about God's mercy reaching a hated enemy, and a challenge to a prophet who resents it.
uncommon: Some Jewish and Christian interpreters have read Jonah as a figure of Israel; the text does not support this.

sections.h: Nineveh in the book of Jonah
sections.b: The book calls Nineveh "the great city" and says it was a three-day walk (Jonah 3:3). Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, in what is now northern Iraq, from about 705 BC. The prophets name it as a symbol of violence (Nahum 3:1; Zephaniah 2:13-15); Genesis 10:11-12 traces its building to Nimrod. In Jonah, Nineveh hears a five-word warning and turns back, from the king to the animals. It fell in 612 BC. Jesus said its people would rise at the judgment to condemn those who did not repent (Matthew 12:41).
sections.refs: Genesis 10:11-12; Jonah 1:2; Jonah 3:3-10; Jonah 4:11; Nahum 3:1; Zephaniah 2:13; Matthew 12:41

sections.h: Tarshish in the book of Jonah
sections.b: Jonah boards a ship "toward Tarshish" to get as far from Nineveh as possible (Jonah 1:3; 4:2). Tarshish is placed in the far west and linked to silver, tin and the largest trading ships (1 Kings 10:22; Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12). Tartessos in Spain is the commonest identification, but Sardinia and north Africa have also been proposed; Josephus took it for Tarsus in Cilicia (Antiquities 1.6.1). The book needs only that it is the opposite direction.
sections.refs: Jonah 1:3; Jonah 4:2; 1 Kings 10:22; Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12; Psalm 72:10

sections.h: The sign of Jonah
sections.b: When some scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, Jesus says no sign will be given "except the sign of Jonah" (Matthew 12:39; 16:4). In Matthew the sign is Jonah's three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, as the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). In Luke it is that "Jonah became a sign for the people of Nineveh" (Luke 11:30), his preaching being the sign. Both add that the people of Nineveh will condemn that generation, because they repented (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32). Readers differ on whether the sign is the resurrection, the preaching, or both, and on how literally to take the "three days and three nights."

common: The sign points to Jesus's death and resurrection (Matthew's reading).
uncommon: Some scholars hold that Matthew 12:40 was added to the saying, and that the original sign was the preaching (Luke).

sections.h: Jonah 3:9-10 and 4:2
sections.b: In Jonah the verb nicham ("change one's mind") is used three times. The king hopes God will "change his mind" (3:9). God does, about the harm he had spoken of doing to Nineveh (3:10). And Jonah quotes the creed (as Joel 2:13 does) that God is "one who changes his mind about the harm" (4:2). The book sets this beside Jeremiah's rule (Jeremiah 18:7-10): a threatened harm is called off if the nation turns back. Jonah's anger is that this principle applies to Assyria.

sections.h: Nineveh turns back
sections.b: The people of Nineveh believe in God, call a fast, put on sackcloth, and turn from their evil way and the violence in their hands (Jonah 3:5-8). The king hopes without presuming: "Who knows?" (3:9; compare 2 Samuel 12:22; Joel 2:14). God sees "their deeds" and changes his mind (3:10). The Mishnah (Ta'anit 2:1) draws the lesson that God sees deeds, not sackcloth. Jesus says Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching (Matthew 12:41).

sections.h: The fast of Nineveh
sections.b: The whole city of Nineveh fasts, "from their great ones to their small ones" (Jonah 3:5), and the king orders that the animals also go without food or drink (3:7). The Coptic Church's Fast of Jonah, the Syriac Rogation of the Ninevites and the Ethiopian Fast of Nineveh recall it before Lent. The Mishnah (Ta'anit 2:1) uses Jonah 3:10 in the liturgy of fast days.

sections.h: Assyria in the book of Jonah
sections.b: Jonah never calls the city Assyria's capital, and the king is "the king of Nineveh," but readers knew that Nineveh's empire had destroyed Samaria (2 Kings 17) and threatened Judah (2 Kings 18-19). Nahum and Zephaniah 2:13-15 announce its fall. Jonah asks what Israel should feel about such an enemy being forgiven.
sections.refs: Jonah 1:2; Jonah 3:6; Jonah 4:2; 2 Kings 14:25; 2 Kings 17:5-6; Nahum 3:1; Zephaniah 2:13

sections.h: A prophet who runs, and a warning that is not carried out
sections.b: Jonah is the one prophet in the Bible said to run from his commission (Jonah 1:3), and his spoken word, "Nineveh will be overturned," was not carried out (3:4, 10). Deuteronomy 18:22 says a prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken for the LORD; Jeremiah 18:7-10 explains that a message of harm is conditional on the people's response. Jonah's complaint (4:2) is that he knew this, and resented it. The book is therefore a central text on what a prophet is for.
sections.refs: Jonah 1:3; Jonah 3:4; Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:2; Deuteronomy 18:22; Jeremiah 18:7-10

sections.h: Prayers in the book of Jonah
sections.b: Jonah has three kinds of prayer. The sailors pray to their own gods, then to the LORD by name (Jonah 1:5, 14). Jonah prays a psalm of thanks from the fish, built from the Psalms (2:2-9). And at the end he prays in anger, quoting the creed (4:2-3). The Ninevites are told to "call out to God with strength" (3:8). The book shows prayer as an act that a foreigner, a prophet or a king can do, and that can be honest and angry as well as grateful.
sections.refs: Jonah 1:5; Jonah 1:14; Jonah 2:1-9; Jonah 3:8; Jonah 4:2-3; Psalm 120:1; Psalm 30:3

sections.h: The sea in the book of Jonah
sections.b: The sea is where Jonah flees (Jonah 1:3), where the LORD hurls a wind (1:4), and the chaos that calms when Jonah goes in (1:15). In his psalm the deep, the breakers and the waves are the LORD's (2:3), echoing Psalm 42:7. The Hebrew poets use the sea for the powers God subdues (Psalm 107:23-30; Habakkuk 3:8); in Jonah the sea obeys God's word, like the fish.
sections.refs: Jonah 1:4; Jonah 1:15; Jonah 2:3-6; Psalm 42:7; Psalm 107:23-30; Habakkuk 3:8

sections.h: The sailors' lot
sections.b: The sailors cast lots to find the cause of the storm, and the lot falls on Jonah (Jonah 1:7). The narrator does not endorse their method, but lets the LORD use it, as Proverbs 16:33 says all lots are the LORD's decision. The earlier lots of Israel (Joshua 7:14-18; 1 Samuel 14:41-42) were part of worship; here the lot is a foreign sailors' practice, and it points exactly.

sections.h: Forgiveness for the enemy
sections.b: Jonah's objection to forgiving Nineveh is the book's drama. The same creed that Moses heard at Sinai (Exodus 34:6-7) is quoted by Jonah as the reason he did not want to go (Jonah 4:2). God's last words to him ask whether he does not have a right to forgive those who do not know right from left (4:11). Micah 7:18-20, read with Jonah on Yom Kippur, praises the God who "pardons guilt" and forgives the remnant.

sections.h: "Should I not have pity on Nineveh?"
sections.b: The book ends with God's question about pity (chus, 4:10-11). Jonah "had pity" on a plant that he did not work for; God asks whether he should not have pity on a city of 120,000 who "do not know the difference between their right hand and their left," and on its animals. Psalm 36:6 says the LORD keeps humans and animals safe. The book makes mercy to outsiders the center of its theology.

sections.h: "Great in loyal love" in Jonah
sections.b: The creed Jonah quotes in 4:2 calls the LORD "slow to anger and great in loyal love." Jonah 2:8 uses the same word, hesed, when it says that those who devote themselves to empty nothings abandon "their loyal love" (a hard Hebrew phrase). The book thus holds that loyal love is God's character and the sailors' and Ninevites' possibility.

sections.h: Foreigners who do better than the prophet
sections.b: The sailors fear the LORD, pray, spare Jonah and make vows (Jonah 1:5-16). The Ninevites believe, fast and turn back (3:5-10). Both do what the prophet at first will not. Peter's words in Acts 10:34-35, that God does not play favorites, are often read beside the book, and Peter was at Joppa when he was sent to Cornelius (Acts 10:5-9).

sections.h: Israel's God and the nations
sections.b: Jonah does not deny that Israel is chosen; Jonah himself is a Hebrew prophet (Jonah 1:9). What it denies is that Israel's election is a reason to hold back the LORD's mercy from others. Readers in different traditions have read it as a challenge to narrow views of election (Acts 10:34-35), or as evidence that the LORD's saving purposes reach the nations through Israel's own prophet.

sections.h: The belly of Sheol
sections.b: In his psalm Jonah calls the fish's insides "the belly of Sheol" and describes the bars of the earth closed behind him (Jonah 2:2, 6). He is speaking of near death by drowning, in the Psalms' language of the pit (Psalm 30:3; Psalm 88:5-6). Jesus compares the Son of Man's time "in the heart of the earth" to Jonah's (Matthew 12:40).

sections.h: Jonah brought up from the Pit
sections.b: The Hebrew of Jonah 2:6, "you brought my life up from the Pit," describes rescue from near death, not resurrection of the dead. Christians have heard more in it since Matthew 12:40, and the fathers took the three days as a sign of Christ's rising. Hosea 6:2 uses the same "after two days ... on the third day" pattern for national revival.

sections.h: Jonah on the Day of Atonement
sections.b: The book of Jonah is read at the afternoon (minchah) service of Yom Kippur (Bavli Megillah 31a); many communities then add Micah 7:18-20. Its themes of repentance and divine pardon, and the reading of a prophet who learns that God forgives even his enemies, are part of the day's liturgy.

sections.h: Jonah as a "sign"
sections.b: Luke 11:30 says "Jonah became a sign for the people of Nineveh," which makes the prophet himself, with his rescue and his preaching, a sign. This differs from prophetic sign acts like Hosea's marriage or Ezekiel's lying on his side, which are done to carry a message, but Matthew and Luke use "sign" in the same sense.

sections.h: Jonah among the Twelve
sections.b: Jonah is the only one of the Twelve that is mostly a story about a prophet and not a collection of his speeches. In the Masoretic order it stands after Obadiah's judgment on Edom and before Micah and Nahum, which announces Nineveh's fall (Nahum 1:1; 3:1); in the Greek order Nahum follows Jonah directly. Jonah 4:2 and Joel 2:13 share the creed of Exodus 34:6, and Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 share the "Who knows?" Readers who see the Twelve as edited into a unit (Nogalski, Schart, Sweeney) count such ties as evidence; Ben Zvi and Barton doubt that they show one book. Whether the Twelve was shaped as one book is debated.
